body_markdown:
A shortage of registered nurses across England's NHS is raising fresh concerns about patient safety, with the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) warning that inadequate staffing can contribute to delays in treatment, missed care and serious incidents involving vulnerable patients.


A new RCN report examining the number of nurses needed across the NHS suggests that England has a substantial gap in its registered nursing workforce. The organisation argues that the shortage is not simply a recruitment issue. It can also have direct consequences for patients and the ability of healthcare workers to provide safe and timely care.


The findings come at a time when hospitals are dealing with significant demand and increasingly complex patient needs. According to the RCN, reports from NHS hospital trusts show that staffing shortages have been associated with incidents such as delayed medication, missed care and delays in providing pain relief.


## Patients waiting for essential care


One of the most serious concerns highlighted by the report is what can happen when nurses are responsible for too many patients at the same time.


Nursing care involves much more than administering medication. Nurses monitor patients, identify changes in their condition, assist people who are at risk of falling, respond to emergencies and ensure essential treatments are delivered. When staffing levels are inadequate, nurses may have to prioritise the most urgent tasks while other aspects of care are delayed.


The RCN's analysis refers to so-called "nursing red flags", which include safety incidents associated with insufficient registered nurse staffing. These can involve delays to medication and pain relief as well as care that is missed or postponed.


The college says that some NHS trusts record hundreds of such incidents during individual months, although it also notes that reporting is inconsistent between organisations. This means the available figures should not necessarily be interpreted as a complete national count of every staffing-related safety incident.


The consequences described by frontline nurses can nevertheless be severe.


One nurse quoted in reporting about the RCN findings described an incident in which an elderly patient fell from a hospital bed during a night shift when staffing levels were low. The patient suffered a brain injury, and a broken hip was reportedly discovered later.


Another nurse described working shifts where having sufficient staff had become unusual, with nurses sometimes caring for around 10 acutely ill patients each.


These accounts illustrate the pressures that can arise when nursing teams are stretched beyond the level required to safely manage patient needs.


## England has tens of thousands fewer nurses than it could have


The RCN's latest report, *In Short Supply: Estimating the shortfall of registered nurses in the NHS in England* , looks at different ways of calculating the size of the nursing workforce gap.


Rather than providing one definitive figure, the report examines several measures of workforce demand. Its overall conclusion is that England has a significant shortage of registered nurses and requires sustained investment in the workforce.


The report highlights the different rates at which the numbers of doctors and nurses have increased over the years.


According to figures cited by the RCN, the number of nurses increased by around 33% between 2009 and the present period examined by the report, while the number of doctors increased by approximately 60%.


Using that comparison, the RCN estimates that England could have more than 77,000 additional nurses if nursing numbers had grown at the same rate as the medical workforce.


The organisation also uses hospital activity as another way of measuring demand. On that basis, it estimates that nursing numbers would be around 55,000 higher if they had kept pace with growth in hospital activity since 2009/10.


These calculations are different measures of the workforce gap rather than separate counts of vacant jobs. They are intended to demonstrate how the number of nurses has changed in relation to other measures of healthcare demand.


## Vacancy figures may not tell the whole story


The report also points to around 23,000 nursing vacancies in England. However, the RCN argues that the official vacancy figure does not necessarily capture the entire workforce shortfall.


For example, a position may be required but remain unfunded or frozen. Such a post would not necessarily appear in conventional vacancy statistics, even though the workforce need remains.


This distinction is important because simply counting advertised vacancies may give a narrower picture of staffing pressures than looking at the number of nurses required to meet patient demand.


The RCN says nursing shortages are also distributed unevenly across England. Some hospitals and regions may face considerably greater staffing pressures than others.


## Increasing pressure on nursing teams


The staffing issue is also connected to the changing nature of healthcare.


Patients entering hospitals can have multiple medical conditions and require more complicated care. At the same time, nurses are expected to manage large caseloads while monitoring patients and responding to unexpected emergencies.


Earlier in 2026, an RCN survey of more than 13,000 nursing staff found that 69% said staffing pressures were forcing them to make difficult decisions about which aspects of care should be prioritised. The survey also found that 79% of respondents believed clinical complexity had increased over the previous two years.


This provides additional context for the latest workforce report.


A shortage does not necessarily mean that every patient will experience poor care. Hospitals can respond by changing staffing arrangements, using temporary workers, moving staff between departments or prioritising patients according to clinical urgency.


However, persistent understaffing can place additional pressure on the nurses who are available.


The RCN has previously highlighted concerns about the relationship between registered nurse staffing levels and patient outcomes. Its recent work on nurse-to-patient ratios argues that minimum staffing levels can act as a safeguard against staffing falling below levels considered necessary for safe care.


## The wider workforce challenge


The debate is not only about recruiting more nurses. Retaining existing staff and ensuring that newly qualified nurses can enter the NHS workforce are also significant issues.


In August 2026, the RCN reported that some newly qualified nurses were encountering difficulties accessing entry-level NHS positions, despite the organisation continuing to highlight nursing vacancies. The college said that at least one-third of entry-level nursing jobs reviewed in England during July required previous experience that could prevent new graduates from applying.


This creates a complicated picture. The NHS can have nursing vacancies while newly qualified nurses struggle to secure suitable first posts.


The RCN has called for workforce planning to be better aligned with education and recruitment, alongside sufficient funding for nursing positions.


## What happens next?


The latest report calls for long-term investment in the registered nursing workforce rather than relying solely on short-term measures.


The organisation argues that workforce planning should take account of patient demand, hospital activity and the complexity of care, rather than focusing only on the number of formally recorded vacancies.


For patients, the central issue is straightforward: hospitals need enough appropriately qualified staff to provide care safely and promptly.


The evidence presented by the RCN suggests that staffing levels can affect whether nurses have enough time to administer medication, respond to patients who need assistance, monitor changes in health and complete essential aspects of care.


The Department of Health and Social Care has been approached for comment on the concerns raised by the report.


The discussion around nurse shortages is likely to continue as NHS organisations attempt to balance increasing demand with workforce and financial constraints. The RCN's report adds to a growing body of evidence and professional commentary focused on whether the current nursing workforce is sufficient for the level of care required.


### Source


Royal College of Nursing, *In Short Supply: Estimating the shortfall of registered nurses in the NHS in England* , published 22 September 2026.
